title: Der Liebste Roland
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 56. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, anfieng, Thüre, gethan, Rath, Wuth, todt und gerieth).
about: KHM 56, a flight-and-transformation tale, and one of the Grimms’ most brutal openings: a witch means to behead her stepdaughter in the night and, misled by a swapped place in the bed, kills her own daughter instead. The girl and her sweetheart Roland escape with the witch’s wand and are pursued through a chain of shapes — lake and duck, flower and fiddler — until the pursuer is danced to death in a thorn hedge. The quieter second half is the stranger one: Roland forgets the girl, and she waits as a red field-stone and then as a flower until her own singing voice brings his memory home. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as gieng, Thüre, gethan, rathe and todt.

sentences.t: Es war einmal eine Frau, die war eine rechte Hexe, und hatte zwei Töchter, eine häßlich und böse, und die liebte sie, weil sie ihre rechte Tochter war, und eine schön und gut, die haßte sie, weil sie ihre Stieftochter war.
sentences.l: There was once a woman who was a right witch, and had two daughters, one ugly and wicked, and that one she loved, because she was her right daughter, and one beautiful and good, that one she hated, because she was her stepdaughter.
sentences.i: There was once a woman who was a true witch, and she had two daughters: one ugly and wicked, and this one she loved, because she was her own child; and one beautiful and good, and this one she hated, because she was her stepdaughter.
sentences.n: recht does double duty here: “eine rechte Hexe” is a thorough-going, proper witch, and “ihre rechte Tochter” is her own true-born daughter.

sentences.t: Zu einer Zeit hatte die Stieftochter eine schöne Schürze, die der andern gefiel, so daß sie neidisch war und ihrer Mutter sagte sie wollte und müßte die Schürze haben.
sentences.l: At one time the stepdaughter had a beautiful apron, which pleased the other, so that she was envious and said to her mother she wanted and must have the apron.
sentences.i: Once the stepdaughter had a beautiful apron which took the other’s fancy, so that she grew envious and told her mother she wanted the apron and must have it.
sentences.n: gefallen turns the sentence round: the apron pleases her, rather than she likes it. müßte is subjunctive — her own words, reported at second hand; wollte can be read either way, the form being the same.

sentences.t: „Sei still, mein Kind,“ sprach die Alte, „du sollst sie auch haben.
sentences.l: “Be still, my child,” spoke the old woman, “you shall have it too.
sentences.i: “Hush, my child,” said the old woman, “and have it you shall.
sentences.n: “die Alte” — the old one — is what the tale calls the witch from here on. auch here is not “also” but a reinforcement of the promise.

sentences.t: Deine Stiefschwester hat längst den Tod verdient, heute Nacht wenn sie schläft, so komm ich und haue ihr den Kopf ab.
sentences.l: Your stepsister has long deserved death, tonight when she sleeps, so come I and hew her head off.
sentences.i: Your stepsister has long deserved to die. Tonight, while she is asleep, I will come and strike her head off.
sentences.n: The present tense (“so komm ich”) stands for the future, as often in spoken German.

sentences.t: Sorge nur daß du hinten ins Bett zu liegen kommst, und schieb sie recht vornen hin.“
sentences.l: See only to it that you come to lie at the back in the bed, and push her right to the front.
sentences.i: Only see to it that you come to lie at the back of the bed, and push her well to the front.
sentences.n: The bed stands against a wall: hinten is the wall side, vornen the open side — which is why the placing decides who dies.

sentences.t: Um das arme Mädchen war es geschehen, wenn es nicht gerade in einer Ecke gestanden und alles mit angehört hätte.
sentences.l: For the poor girl it would have been all over, if she had not just been standing in a corner and listened in on the whole of it.
sentences.i: It would have been all over with the poor girl, had she not chanced to be standing in a corner and heard everything.
sentences.n: “um jemanden ist es geschehen” = someone is done for. Mädchen is grammatically neuter, so German calls the girl es (“it”) all through the tale, with sein for “her” — we use “she” in English. “alles mit anhören” = to listen in on the whole of it.

sentences.t: Es durfte den ganzen Tag nicht zur Thüre hinaus, und als Schlafenszeit gekommen war, mußte es zuerst ins Bett steigen, damit sie sich hinten hin legen konnte; als sie aber eingeschlafen war, da schob es sie sachte vornen hin und nahm den Platz hinten an der Wand.
sentences.l: She was not allowed out the door the whole day, and when sleeping-time had come, she had to climb into the bed first, so that the other could lay herself at the back; but when she had fallen asleep, then pushed she her gently to the front and took the place at the back by the wall.
sentences.i: All day she was not allowed out of doors; and when bedtime came she had to get into bed first, so that the other could lie down at the back. But once the other was asleep, she pushed her gently to the front and took the place at the back against the wall.
sentences.n: Two girls and two pronouns: es is the stepdaughter, sie the witch’s own daughter. German keeps them apart by gender where English cannot.

sentences.t: In der Nacht kam die Alte geschlichen, in der rechten Hand hielt sie eine Axt, mit der linken fühlte sie erst ob auch jemand vornen lag, und dann faßte sie die Axt mit beiden Händen, hieb und hieb ihrem eigenen Kinde den Kopf ab.
sentences.l: In the night came the old woman creeping, in the right hand she held an axe, with the left she felt first whether anyone really lay at the front, and then she grasped the axe with both hands, hewed and hewed her own child’s head off.
sentences.i: In the night the old woman came creeping. In her right hand she held an axe; with her left she first felt whether someone really was lying at the front, and then she took the axe in both hands and hewed, and hewed her own child’s head off.
sentences.n: auch inside the ob-clause means “really, sure enough.” The doubled “hieb und hieb” spares the reader nothing, and is meant not to.

sentences.t: Als sie fort gegangen war, stand das Mädchen auf, und gieng zu seinem Liebsten, der Roland hieß, und klopfte an seine Thüre.
sentences.l: When she had gone away, the girl got up, and went to her sweetheart, who was called Roland, and knocked at his door.
sentences.n: Liebster is a superlative used as a noun — “the dearest one,” hence sweetheart; it gives the tale its title. The possessive is the neuter seinem because Mädchen is neuter, though it means “her.”

sentences.t: Als er heraus kam, sprach sie zu ihm „höre, liebster Roland, wir müssen eilig flüchten, die Stiefmutter hat mich todtschlagen wollen, hat aber ihr eigenes Kind getroffen.
sentences.l: When he came out, she spoke to him “listen, dearest Roland, we must flee in haste, the stepmother wanted to strike me dead, but has hit her own child.
sentences.i: When he came out she said to him: “Listen, dearest Roland, we must flee at once — my stepmother meant to strike me dead, but she has struck her own child instead.
sentences.n: “hat… wollen” — with a modal, the perfect takes the infinitive wollen instead of the participle gewollt; this double infinitive is standard German.

sentences.t: Kommt der Tag, und sie sieht was sie gethan hat, so sind wir verloren.“
sentences.l: Comes the day, and she sees what she has done, so are we lost.”
sentences.i: When day comes and she sees what she has done, we are lost.”
sentences.n: A conditional clause with no wenn: the verb simply comes first — “Kommt der Tag” = if/when day comes.

sentences.t: „Aber ich rathe dir,“ sagte Roland, „daß du erst ihren Zauberstab wegnimmst, sonst können wir uns nicht retten, wenn sie uns nachsetzt und verfolgt.“
sentences.l: “But I advise you,” said Roland, “that you first take her magic-wand away, otherwise we cannot save ourselves, if she sets after us and pursues.”
sentences.i: “But my advice,” said Roland, “is that you first take her wand away, or we cannot save ourselves when she comes after us in pursuit.”
sentences.n: rathe = modern rate, the same th- as in Rath. nachsetzen is to give chase.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen holte den Zauberstab, und dann nahm es den todten Kopf und tröpfelte drei Blutstropfen auf die Erde, einen vors Bett, einen in die Küche, und einen auf die Treppe.
sentences.l: The girl fetched the magic-wand, and then took she the dead head and dripped three drops of blood onto the earth, one before the bed, one in the kitchen, and one on the stairs.
sentences.i: The girl fetched the wand, and then took the dead head and let three drops of blood fall on the ground — one before the bed, one in the kitchen, and one on the stairs.
sentences.n: vors = vor das. Blood that speaks for its owner is an old motif; three drops of a mother’s blood go with the bride in KHM 89.

sentences.t: Darauf eilte es mit seinem Liebsten fort.
sentences.l: Thereupon hurried she away with her sweetheart.
sentences.i: Then she hurried away with her sweetheart.

sentences.t: Als nun am Morgen die alte Hexe aufgestanden war, rief sie ihrer Tochter, und wollte ihr die Schürze geben, aber sie kam nicht.
sentences.l: When now in the morning the old witch had got up, she called to her daughter, and wanted to give her the apron, but she did not come.
sentences.i: Now when the old witch had got up in the morning, she called her daughter, meaning to give her the apron; but she did not come.
sentences.n: “rief sie ihrer Tochter” — rufen with the dative, an older construction: to call to someone.

sentences.t: Da rief sie „wo bist du?“
sentences.l: Then called she “where are you?”
sentences.i: Then she called: “Where are you?”

sentences.t: „Ei, hier auf der Treppe, da kehr ich,“ antwortete der eine Blutstropfen.
sentences.l: “Why, here on the stairs, I am sweeping,” answered the one drop of blood.
sentences.i: “Why, here on the stairs — I am sweeping,” answered the first drop of blood.
sentences.n: kehren is to sweep. “der eine… der zweite… der dritte” counts them off: the one, the second, the third. Ei is a small exclamation of surprise.

sentences.t: Die Alte gieng hinaus, sah aber niemand auf der Treppe und rief abermals „wo bist du?“
sentences.l: The old woman went out, but saw nobody on the stairs and called once again “where are you?”

sentences.t: „Ei, hier in der Küche, da wärm ich mich“ rief der zweite Blutstropfen.
sentences.l: “Why, here in the kitchen, I am warming myself,” called the second drop of blood.

sentences.t: Sie gieng in die Küche, aber sie fand niemand.
sentences.l: She went into the kitchen, but she found nobody.

sentences.t: Da rief sie noch einmal „wo bist du?“
sentences.l: Then called she once more “where are you?”
sentences.i: Then she called once more: “Where are you?”

sentences.t: „Ach, hier im Bette, da schlaf ich“ rief der dritte Blutstropfen.
sentences.l: “Ah, here in the bed, I am sleeping,” called the third drop of blood.

sentences.t: Sie gieng in die Kammer ans Bett.
sentences.l: She went into the chamber to the bed.

sentences.t: Was sah sie da? ihr eigenes Kind, das in seinem Blute schwamm, und dem sie selbst den Kopf abgehauen hatte.
sentences.l: What saw she there? her own child, which swam in its blood, and whose head she herself had hewn off.
sentences.i: What did she see there? Her own child, swimming in its blood, whose head she herself had struck off.
sentences.n: The 1857 text runs straight on after the question mark with a lower-case ihr, and we keep it. “dem sie den Kopf abgehauen hatte” puts the person in the dative: the head was hewn off her.

sentences.t: Die Hexe gerieth in Wuth, sprang ans Fenster, und da sie weit in die Welt schauen konnte, erblickte sie ihre Stieftochter, die mit ihrem Liebsten Roland fort eilte.
sentences.l: The witch fell into fury, sprang to the window, and since she could look far out into the world, she caught sight of her stepdaughter, who was hurrying away with her sweetheart Roland.
sentences.i: The witch flew into a fury and sprang to the window; and since she could see far out into the world, she caught sight of her stepdaughter hurrying away with her sweetheart Roland.
sentences.n: The far sight is given without explanation — she simply can see to the horizon, being what she is.

sentences.t: „Das soll euch nichts helfen,“ rief sie, „wenn ihr auch schon weit weg seid, ihr entflieht mir doch nicht.“
sentences.l: “That shall help you nothing,” cried she, “even if you are already far away, you will not escape me all the same.”
sentences.i: “That shall do you no good,” she cried. “Far off as you already are, you shall not escape me.”
sentences.n: “wenn… auch schon” = even if, even though. entfliehen takes the dative of the person fled from (mir).

sentences.t: Sie zog ihre Meilenstiefeln an, in welchem sie mit jedem Schritt eine Stunde machte, und es dauerte nicht lange, so hatte sie beide eingeholt.
sentences.l: She drew on her mile-boots, in which she made an hour with every step, and it did not last long, so had she overtaken them both.
sentences.i: She drew on her league-boots, in which every stride carried her an hour’s journey; and it was not long before she had overtaken them both.
sentences.n: Meilenstiefel are boots that stride miles at a time. An hour is here a measure of distance — as far as a person walks in one. The 1857 text has “in welchem,” singular, where the plural welchen would be expected after Stiefeln; whether that is a printer’s slip or a loose older agreement is not clear.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen aber, wie es die Alte daher schreiten sah, verwandelte mit dem Zauberstab seinen Liebsten Roland in einen See, sich selbst aber in eine Ente, die mitten auf dem See schwamm.
sentences.l: The girl however, when she saw the old woman striding up, transformed with the magic-wand her sweetheart Roland into a lake, but herself into a duck that swam in the middle of the lake.
sentences.i: But the girl, when she saw the old woman come striding up, turned her sweetheart Roland with the wand into a lake, and herself into a duck that swam in the middle of it.
sentences.n: “daher schreiten” is to come striding along; sah takes a bare infinitive, as English “saw her come.”

sentences.t: Die Hexe stellte sich ans Ufer, warf Brotbrocken hinein und gab sich alle Mühe die Ente herbeizulocken: aber die Ente ließ sich nicht locken, und die Alte mußte Abends unverrichteter Sache wieder umkehren.
sentences.l: The witch placed herself at the bank, threw bread-crumbs in and gave herself every trouble to lure the duck over: but the duck let itself not be lured, and the old woman had to turn back in the evening with her business unaccomplished.
sentences.i: The witch stationed herself on the bank, threw in crumbs of bread and took every pains to lure the duck to her; but the duck would not be lured, and in the evening the old woman had to turn back with nothing accomplished.
sentences.n: “sich alle Mühe geben” = to take every pains. “unverrichteter Sache” is a fixed genitive phrase: with the business undone, empty-handed.

sentences.t: Darauf nahm das Mädchen mit seinem Liebsten Roland wieder die natürliche Gestalt an, und sie giengen die ganze Nacht weiter bis zu Tagesanbruch.
sentences.l: Thereupon took the girl with her sweetheart Roland the natural shape on again, and they went on the whole night until daybreak.
sentences.i: Then the girl and her sweetheart Roland took their natural shape again, and they walked on all night until daybreak.

sentences.t: Da verwandelte sich das Mädchen in eine schöne Blume, die mitten in einer Dornhecke stand, seinen Liebsten Roland aber in einen Geigenspieler.
sentences.l: Then transformed the girl herself into a beautiful flower that stood in the middle of a thorn-hedge, but her sweetheart Roland into a fiddle-player.
sentences.i: Then the girl turned herself into a beautiful flower standing in the midst of a thorn hedge, and her sweetheart Roland into a fiddler.
sentences.n: One verb serves both halves — reflexive for herself, transitive for him: “verwandelte sich… in eine Blume, seinen Liebsten aber in einen Geigenspieler.”

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so kam die Hexe herangeschritten und sprach zu dem Spielmann „lieber Spielmann, darf ich mir wohl die schöne Blume abbrechen?“
sentences.l: Not long, so came the witch striding up and spoke to the minstrel “dear minstrel, may I well break off the beautiful flower for myself?”
sentences.i: Before long the witch came striding up and said to the minstrel: “Dear minstrel, might I break off that beautiful flower for myself?”
sentences.n: Spielmann is the old word for a travelling musician. The dative mir in “mir abbrechen” marks that she plucks it for her own.

sentences.t: „O ja,“ antwortete er, „ich will dazu aufspielen.“
sentences.l: “Oh yes,” answered he, “I will strike up to it.”
sentences.i: “Oh yes,” he answered, “and I will play a tune to it.”
sentences.n: aufspielen is to strike up, to start playing; dazu = to accompany the doing of it.

sentences.t: Als sie nun mit Hast in die Hecke kroch und die Blume brechen wollte, denn sie wußte wohl wer die Blume war, so fieng er an aufzuspielen, und, sie mochte wollen oder nicht, sie mußte tanzen, denn es war ein Zaubertanz.
sentences.l: When she now crept with haste into the hedge and wanted to break the flower, for she knew well who the flower was, so began he to strike up, and, she might want to or not, she had to dance, for it was a magic-dance.
sentences.i: Now when she crept in haste into the hedge and made to pluck the flower — for she knew well who the flower was — he struck up his tune; and whether she would or not, she had to dance, for it was a dance of enchantment.
sentences.n: “sie mochte wollen oder nicht” = whether she wanted to or not. The German asks wer die Blume war, who and not what: inside the flower the girl is still a person.

sentences.t: Je schneller er spielte, desto gewaltigere Sprünge mußte sie machen, und die Dornen rissen ihr die Kleider vom Leibe, stachen sie blutig und wund, und da er nicht aufhörte, mußte sie so lange tanzen bis sie todt liegen blieb.
sentences.l: The faster he played, the mightier leaps had she to make, and the thorns tore her the clothes from the body, stabbed her bloody and sore, and since he did not stop, she had to dance so long until she stayed lying dead.
sentences.i: The faster he played, the higher she had to leap; and the thorns tore the clothes from her body and pricked her bloody and raw; and since he did not stop, she had to dance until she fell and lay dead.
sentences.n: “je… desto…” is the standard German “the… the…”. “todt liegen blieb” — she stayed lying dead; the tale watches the whole of it rather than looking away.

sentences.t: Als sie nun erlöst waren, sprach Roland „nun will ich zu meinem Vater gehen und die Hochzeit bestellen.“
sentences.l: When they were now delivered, spoke Roland “now will I go to my father and arrange the wedding.”
sentences.i: Now that they were delivered, Roland said: “Now I will go to my father and arrange the wedding.”
sentences.n: erlöst — released, delivered; the same weighty word used elsewhere of breaking an enchantment. bestellen here is to order a thing, to see it arranged.

sentences.t: „So will ich derweil hier bleiben,“ sagte das Mädchen, „und auf dich warten, und damit mich niemand erkennt, will ich mich in einen rothen Feldstein verwandeln.“
sentences.l: “Then will I stay here meanwhile,” said the girl, “and wait for you, and so that nobody recognizes me, I will transform myself into a red field-stone.”
sentences.i: “Then I will stay here meanwhile,” said the girl, “and wait for you; and so that nobody shall know me, I will turn myself into a red field-stone.”
sentences.n: derweil = meanwhile. A Feldstein is a loose stone lying out in a field, of no interest to anyone — which is the point.

sentences.t: Da gieng Roland fort, und das Mädchen stand als ein rother Stein auf dem Felde und wartete auf seinen Liebsten.
sentences.l: Then went Roland away, and the girl stood as a red stone in the field and waited for her sweetheart.
sentences.i: Then Roland went away, and the girl stood as a red stone in the field and waited for her sweetheart.

sentences.t: Als aber Roland heim kam, gerieth er in die Fallstricke einer andern, die es dahin brachte, daß er das Mädchen vergaß.
sentences.l: But when Roland came home, he fell into the snares of another, who brought it so far that he forgot the girl.
sentences.i: But when Roland came home he fell into the snares of another woman, who brought things so far that he forgot the girl.
sentences.n: Fallstrick is a snare or gin set for game, used here of a woman’s wiles. “es dahin bringen, daß…” = to bring things to the point that.

sentences.t: Das arme Mädchen stand lange Zeit, als er aber endlich gar nicht wieder kam, so ward es traurig und verwandelte sich in eine Blume und dachte „es wird ja wohl einer daher gehen und mich umtreten.“
sentences.l: The poor girl stood a long time, but when he at last did not come again at all, so grew she sad and transformed herself into a flower and thought “surely someone will come along here and tread me down.”
sentences.i: The poor girl stood there a long while; but when at last he did not come back at all, she grew sad and turned herself into a flower, and thought: “Surely someone will come along and trample me underfoot.”
sentences.n: “es wird ja wohl einer…” — the future here is a resigned guess rather than a prediction. She chooses the flower expecting to be destroyed in it.

sentences.t: Es trug sich aber zu, daß ein Schäfer auf dem Felde seine Schafe hütete und die Blume sah, und weil sie so schön war, so brach er sie ab, nahm sie mit sich, und legte sie in seinen Kasten.
sentences.l: But it came to pass that a shepherd was tending his sheep in the field and saw the flower, and because it was so beautiful, so he broke it off, took it with him, and laid it in his chest.
sentences.i: But it came to pass that a shepherd was pasturing his sheep in the field and saw the flower; and because it was so beautiful he plucked it, took it with him, and laid it in his chest.
sentences.n: Kasten is a wooden chest or box for clothes and goods.

sentences.t: Von der Zeit gieng es wunderlich in des Schäfers Hause zu.
sentences.l: From that time it went strangely on in the shepherd’s house.
sentences.i: From that time on strange things went on in the shepherd’s house.
sentences.n: zugehen — “es geht zu” — is the verb for how things go on, what happens. “des Schäfers Hause” sets the genitive before its noun and keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Wenn er Morgens aufstand, so war schon alle Arbeit gethan: die Stube war gekehrt, Tisch und Bänke abgeputzt, Feuer auf den Herd gemacht, und Wasser getragen; und Mittags, wenn er heim kam, war der Tisch gedeckt und ein gutes Essen aufgetragen.
sentences.l: When he got up in the mornings, so was all the work already done: the room was swept, table and benches wiped clean, fire made on the hearth, and water carried; and at middays, when he came home, the table was laid and a good meal served up.
sentences.i: When he got up in the morning all the work was already done: the room swept, table and benches wiped clean, a fire made on the hearth and water carried; and at noon, when he came home, the table was laid and a good meal set out.
sentences.n: Morgens and Mittags are old genitives doing adverb duty: of a morning, at noon. Through the list the auxiliary war is left to be understood with each item.

sentences.t: Er konnte nicht begreifen wie das zugieng, denn er sah niemals einen Menschen in seinem Haus, und es konnte sich auch niemand in der kleinen Hütte versteckt haben.
sentences.l: He could not grasp how that came about, for he never saw a person in his house, and nobody could have hidden himself in the little hut either.
sentences.i: He could not make out how it came about, for he never saw a soul in his house, and nobody could have hidden in the little hut either.

sentences.t: Die gute Aufwartung gefiel ihm freilich, aber zuletzt ward ihm doch angst, so daß er zu einer weisen Frau gieng und sie um Rath fragte.
sentences.l: The good attendance pleased him well enough, but at last it grew fearful to him after all, so that he went to a wise woman and asked her for counsel.
sentences.i: The good service pleased him well enough, but in the end he grew frightened all the same, and went to a wise woman and asked her advice.
sentences.n: “ward ihm angst” is the impersonal construction with the person in the dative: fear came upon him. A weise Frau is the village cunning-woman, consulted for exactly this kind of trouble.

sentences.t: Die weise Frau sprach „es steckt Zauberei dahinter; gib einmal Morgens in aller Frühe acht ob sich etwas in der Stube regt, und wenn du etwas siehst, es mag sein was es will, so wirf schnell ein weißes Tuch darüber, dann wird der Zauber gehemmt.“
sentences.l: The wise woman spoke “there is sorcery stuck behind it; give heed once in the morning in all earliness whether something stirs in the room, and if you see something, be it what it may, so throw a white cloth quickly over it, then is the magic checked.”
sentences.i: The wise woman said: “There is sorcery behind it. Take heed early in the morning whether anything stirs in the room; and if you see something, be it what it may, throw a white cloth quickly over it, and the spell will be checked.”
sentences.n: “acht geben” = to take heed. “es mag sein was es will” = be it what it may. “in aller Frühe” = at the very earliest hour. What the white cloth is for is left unexplained; the tale simply takes it that covering an enchanted thing holds the magic still.

sentences.t: Der Schäfer that wie sie gesagt hatte, und am andern Morgen, eben als der Tag anbrach, sah er wie sich der Kasten aufthat und die Blume heraus kam.
sentences.l: The shepherd did as she had said, and the next morning, just as the day broke, he saw how the chest opened itself and the flower came out.
sentences.i: The shepherd did as she had said; and the next morning, just as day was breaking, he saw the chest open of itself and the flower come out.
sentences.n: that and aufthat keep the old th- of thun (modern tat, auftat). German narrates perception with a wie-clause where English says “saw the chest open.”

sentences.t: Schnell sprang er hinzu und warf ein weißes Tuch darüber.
sentences.l: Quickly sprang he to it and threw a white cloth over it.
sentences.i: Quickly he sprang to it and threw a white cloth over it.

sentences.t: Alsbald war die Verwandlung vorbei, und ein schönes Mädchen stand vor ihm, das bekannte ihm daß es die Blume gewesen wäre und seinen Haushalt bisher besorgt hätte.
sentences.l: At once the transformation was over, and a beautiful girl stood before him, who confessed to him that she had been the flower and had looked after his household until now.
sentences.i: At once the transformation was undone, and a beautiful girl stood before him; and she confessed to him that she had been the flower and had kept his house until then.
sentences.n: das (“who”) is the neuter relative, agreeing with Mädchen. gewesen wäre and besorgt hätte are the subjunctive of reported speech: her account of it.

sentences.t: Es erzählte ihm sein Schicksal, und weil es ihm gefiel, fragte er ob es ihn heirathen wollte, aber es antwortete „nein,“ denn es wollte seinem Liebsten Roland, obgleich er es verlassen hatte, doch treu bleiben: aber es versprach daß es nicht weggehen, sondern ihm fernerhin Haus halten wollte.
sentences.l: She told him her fate, and because she pleased him, he asked whether she wanted to marry him, but she answered “no,” for she wanted to stay true to her sweetheart Roland, although he had forsaken her, all the same: but she promised that she would not go away, but rather would keep house for him henceforth.
sentences.i: She told him her story; and because she pleased him he asked whether she would marry him, but she answered “no” — for she meant to stay true to her sweetheart Roland, although he had forsaken her. But she promised that she would not go away, and would keep house for him from now on.
sentences.n: heirathen = modern heiraten. “Haus halten” = to keep house; fernerhin = henceforth.

sentences.t: Nun kam die Zeit heran daß Roland Hochzeit halten sollte: da ward nach altem Brauch im Lande bekannt gemacht daß alle Mädchen sich einfinden und zu Ehren des Brautpaars singen sollten.
sentences.l: Now drew the time near that Roland was to hold his wedding: then it was made known through the land after old custom that all the girls should present themselves and sing in honour of the bridal pair.
sentences.i: Now the time drew near for Roland to hold his wedding; and by old custom it was proclaimed through the land that all the maidens should present themselves and sing in honour of the bridal pair.
sentences.n: “sich einfinden” = to present oneself, to turn up. “nach altem Brauch” = according to old custom.

sentences.t: Das treue Mädchen, als es davon hörte, ward so traurig daß es meinte das Herz im Leib würde ihm zerspringen, und wollte nicht hingehen, aber die andern kamen und holten es herbei.
sentences.l: The faithful girl, when she heard of it, grew so sad that she thought the heart in her body would burst apart, and did not want to go there, but the others came and fetched her along.
sentences.i: When the faithful girl heard of it she grew so sad that she thought the heart in her body would burst; and she would not go, but the others came and fetched her along.
sentences.n: “das Herz im Leib würde ihm zerspringen” — ihm, the neuter dative, is “to her,” the girl; German says the heart would burst to her.

sentences.t: Wenn aber die Reihe kam daß es singen sollte, so trat es zurück, bis es allein noch übrig war, da konnte es nicht anders.
sentences.l: But when the turn came that she should sing, so stepped she back, until she alone was still left over, then could she not otherwise.
sentences.i: But whenever the turn came for her to sing she stepped back, until she alone was left, and then she could do no other.
sentences.n: wenn here is “whenever,” for a thing that happens again and again. “sie konnte nicht anders” = she had no choice.

sentences.t: Aber wie es seinen Gesang anfieng, und er zu Rolands Ohren kam, so sprang er auf, und rief „die Stimme kenne ich, das ist die rechte Braut, eine andere begehr ich nicht.“
sentences.l: But as she began her song, and it came to Roland’s ears, so sprang he up, and cried “the voice I know, that is the right bride, another I desire not.”
sentences.i: But as she began her song, and it came to Roland’s ears, he sprang up and cried: “That voice I know — that is the true bride; no other will I have.”
sentences.n: The er in “und er zu Rolands Ohren kam” is the Gesang, the song, not Roland. rechte returns in its sense of true, rightful — the word that opened the tale.

sentences.t: Alles, was er vergessen hatte und ihm aus dem Sinn verschwunden war, das war plötzlich in sein Herz wieder heim gekommen.
sentences.l: Everything that he had forgotten and that had vanished from his mind, that had suddenly come home again into his heart.
sentences.i: Everything he had forgotten, that had vanished out of his mind, had suddenly come home again into his heart.
sentences.n: Memory here does not simply return: “wieder heim gekommen” is what is said of a person coming home to the house.

sentences.t: Da hielt das treue Mädchen Hochzeit mit seinem Liebsten Roland, und war sein Leid zu Ende und fieng seine Freude an.
sentences.l: Then held the faithful girl her wedding with her sweetheart Roland, and her sorrow was at an end and her joy began.
sentences.i: Then the faithful girl held her wedding with her sweetheart Roland, and her sorrow was at an end and her joy began.
sentences.n: The two closing clauses balance against each other, each with the verb first: “war sein Leid zu Ende und fieng seine Freude an.” sein is “her” both times, the neuter of Mädchen.
